editorial.headline: Care Without Residence: The Scope of KBLI 88102
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 88102 is a nonprofit social-care activity for older people and people with disabilities, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, subject to address verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 88102 concerns social care provided without accommodation for older people and people with disabilities. Its work can take place in a person’s home or another setting, bringing together social services, counselling, welfare support, referrals and related assistance. The scope is practical as well as relational: visits, day-care, help with activities of daily living, social rehabilitation, habilitation and vocational work for people with disabilities all sit within it. The educational component of that vocational work is expressly limited. It also includes care activities and home nursing when delivered as part of home-care services.

The activity is organised by a nonprofit Social Welfare Institution. That institutional character matters because the scope describes a continuing care function rather than a single, isolated service. It reaches into the ordinary routines that can determine whether an older person or a person with a disability can remain supported at home or participate more fully in daily life. The record does not list business-scale categories open to this activity, so it offers no separate scale-based position to add to the definition.

Nationally, the picture is open. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, the national record allows full foreign ownership rather than imposing a partial foreign-equity cap. That clarity should not be diluted by assumptions about service format: the activity remains defined by nonprofit social-welfare provision for the specified people and by the services set out in its scope.

Bali presents a different, but not prohibitive, reading. The record places the activity at medium-high/high risk and says it is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. It is therefore not accurate to say that a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today on that moratorium basis. Nor is this an address-free conclusion: the record calls for verification for the proposed address. The honest position is straightforward—national foreign ownership is open up to 100%, and Bali does not presently block this activity under the moratorium, while the specific location still needs to be checked.
